rv.q: Mr. Shalhoub and Mr. Fontana’s shimmering performances are reason enough to celebrate — and to heave a sigh of relief.

Theater has turned Moss Hart's cracking memoir "Act One" into a rollicking play, which, if you think about it, is the natural medium for a man who lived and breathed the theater, what he called "a lifelong infection."
The result is a thrillingly well-staged play that runs for two hours and 40 minutes but feels much shorter.
As 'Act One' would have it, no love is quite so intense and tempestuous as that between a playwright and his play.

If the portrayal of this bromance, grounded in the frustration and resolve of shared creative work, can bring a new generation of theater people to Hart’s indelible memoir, then Lapine’s production will have been worth the effort.
Lapine's stage adaptation of Hart's sprawling tale is quite faithful and wrought with abundant skill and empathy.
It’s just busy build-up and no emotional payoff, like a musical without the numbers.
Watching James Lapine's long, laborious and, well, hackneyed, Lincoln Center adaptation of Hart'
Delicious star turns from Tony Shalhoub and Santino Fontana can't save this verbose, unwieldy adaptation of Moss Hart's classic autobiography.
If you think watching paint dry is boring, try watching two men edit a long-forgotten play.
So much love and care and ambition have been poured into 'Act One,' playwright/director James Lapine's sprawling stage adaptation of playwright/director Moss Hart's celebrated 1959 memoir.
However, that doesn’t soften the arduousness of sitting through writer-director James Lapine‘s botched attempt at it.
When I say Lapine packs plenty into his entertaining diversion about the dogged fulfillment of concentrated ambition, I mean plenty.
The bitterest disappointment of the Broadway season.

Lapine's Act One (* * * out of four stars), which opened Thursday at Lincoln Center's Theatre, doesn't match the inspired zaniness that was Hart's ideal and trademark — but its creator doesn't seem to be going for that.
Act One is a memory play in the truest sense, filtered through the rose-colored glasses of nostalgia and suffused with the warm glow of what might have been.
Instead of an inspiring account of talent and tenacity, Lapine's “Act One” is a bland story that fails to put Hart’s life into perspective.
It never reveals what made Hart special.
The lack of drama generated on stage about the fate of “Once in a Lifetime” constitutes a major disappointment.
While it does capture Hart’s passion for the theater and offers many pleasures, the play is more than a tad long and rambling.
If they're not, it's hard to see what they'll find to savor - other than a delightful performance by Tony Shalhoub

cn.t: James Lapine's adaptation of Moss Hart's beloved memoir draws praise for Tony Shalhoub's performance and Beowulf Boritt's spectacular set, but critics find the production overstuffed and dramatically inert, struggling to capture the book's magic.

sg.ra: Thrust stage projects into the audience here, so front-center puts you directly in the actors' playing space with 180-degree eye contact. However, SeatPlan and JK's TheatreScene both warn the thrust's elevated downstage lip can obscure upstage action, and the shallow rake this close means you look up at performers working the far edge of the thrust.

At the middle of the thrust's semicircle, the stadium-style rake lifts you over heads in front while the curved row geometry keeps you square to the playing area — the thrust no longer feels side-on because you're on its central axis. SeatPlan, Headout, TickPick and Broadway Scene all converge on D-K center as the best sightlines in the house.

Sits on the central axis of the thrust so you see the three-sided staging in balance rather than from an angle. LCT's official chart confirms Row P has a dedicated step-up giving it elevation above Row O, and Headout lists L, P, O, K as the value-balance rows. At a thrust stage, back-center beats side-front because you read the full geometry of audience-wrapping blocking.

On a thrust stage, the far-side Orchestra seats end up looking ACROSS the playing space rather than at it — you see actors' profiles and often stare at the back of the thrust's far edge. SeatPlan: 'restricted views depending on staging.' JK's TheatreScene explicitly warns 'avoid the 4 or 5 seats closest to the wall.' BWW Forum thread 1082386 exists specifically because patrons worry about side-seat restriction at this venue.

The elevated Loge wraps the same semicircle as the Orchestra but 2 flights up (LCT: 30 steps), giving you the map-view of the thrust's three-sided blocking that's impossible from Orchestra. TickPick: 'Center, in the first three rows' is premium. SeatPlan confirms 'no bar or obstructions' at the front edge. For a thrust stage this is arguably a better seat than Orchestra for geometry-heavy stagings.

Only 5 rows exist in the Loge, so 'back Loge' is still close. TickPick: 'Rows D and E of Center Left and Center Right offer amazing views at a lower cost.' JK's TheatreScene paid $99 for similar seats and called them 'budget-friendly and worth every penny... view not appreciably different than the first few rows.' Elevated angle reads the thrust's three-sided blocking well even from slight side.

Compounds both weaknesses of a thrust-stage venue: you're on the far side of the semicircle AND at the back of the elevated tier, so the upstage portion of the thrust turns away from you. TickPick names Loge R Row E Seat 509 as the worked example: 'the rear end of the stage is going to be obstructed.' SeatPlan: 'Views from the Loge can feel distant, especially at the far sides.'
